CHAPTER XV

Where is the woman that cannot act a part? Where is she who will not
do it, and do it well, to save the man she loves? Nature on these great
occasions comes to the aid of the simplest of the sex, and teaches her
to throw dust in Solomon's eyes. The men had no sooner retired than
Margaret stepped out of bed, and opened the long chest on which she had
been lying down in her skirt and petticoat and stockings, and nightdress
over all; and put the lid, bed-clothes and all, against the wall: then
glided to the door and listened. The footsteps died away through her
father's room and down the stairs.

Now in that chest there was a peculiarity that it was almost impossible
for a stranger to detect. A part of the boarding of the room had been
broken, and Gerard being applied to to make it look neater, and being
short of materials, had ingeniously sawed away a space sufficient just
to admit Margaret's soi-disant bed, and with the materials thus acquired
he had repaired the whole room. As for the bed or chest, it really
rested on the rafters a foot below the boards. Consequently it was full
two feet deep, though it looked scarce one.

All was quiet. Margaret kneeled and gave thanks to Heaven. Then she
glided from the door and leaned over the chest, and whispered tenderly,
“Gerard!”

Gerard did not reply.

She then whispered a little louder, “Gerard, all is safe, thank Heaven!
You may rise; but oh! be cautious!”

Gerard made no reply.

She laid her hand upon his shoulder--“Gerard!”

No reply.

“Oh, what is this?” she cried, and her hands ran wildly over his face
and his bosom. She took him by the shoulders; she shook him; she lifted
him; but he escaped from her trembling hands, and fell back, not like a
man, but like a body. A great dread fell on her. The lid had been down.
She had lain upon it. The men had been some time in the room. With all
the strength of frenzy she tore him out of the chest. She bore him in
her arms to the window. She dashed the window open. The sweet air came
in. She laid him in it and in the moonlight. His face was the colour of
ashes; his body was all limp and motionless. She felt his heart. Horror!
it was as still as the rest! Horror of horrors! she had stifled him with
her own body.

The mind cannot all at once believe so great and sudden and strange a
calamity. Gerard, who had got alive into that chest scarce five minutes
ago, how could he be dead?

She called him by all the endearing names that heart could think or
tongue could frame. She kissed him and fondled him and coaxed him and
implored him to speak to her.

No answer to words of love, such as she had never uttered to him before,
nor thought she could utter. Then the poor creature, trembling all over,
began to say over that ashy face little foolish things that were at once
terrible and pitiable.

“Oh, Gerard! I am very sorry you are dead. I am very sorry I have killed
you. Forgive me for not letting the men take you; it would have been
better than this. Oh, Gerard! I am very, very sorry for what I have
done.” Then she began suddenly to rave.

“No! no! such things can't be, or there is no God. It is monstrous. How
can my Gerard be dead? How can I have killed my Gerard? I love him. Oh,
God! you know how I love him. He does not. I never told him. If he knew
my heart, he would speak to me, he would not be so deaf to his poor
Margaret. It is all a trick to make me cry out and betray him; but no!
I love him too well for that. I'll choke first.” And she seized her own
throat, to check her wild desire to scream in her terror and anguish.

“If he would but say one word. Oh, Gerard! don't die without a word.
Have mercy on me and scold me, but speak to me: if you are angry with
me, scold me! curse me! I deserve it: the idiot that killed the man she
loved better than herself. Ah I am a murderess. The worst in all the
world. Help! help! I have murdered him. Ah! ah! ah! ah! ah!”

She tore her hair, and uttered shriek after shriek, so wild, so
piercing, they fell like a knell upon the ears of Dierich Brower and his
men. All started to their feet and looked at one another.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER TWO.
[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

Where is the woman who cannot perform the role demanded of her? Where is she who refuses to play the part, yet fails to execute it with the necessary artifice to save the life of the man she adores? In moments of such catastrophic gravity, nature itself seems to conspire against the simplicity of the female spirit, forcing her to scatter dust in the eyes of Solomon, blinding reason with the grit of despair.

As the male figures withdrew, retreating into the shadows of their own rooms and descending the stairwell, Margaret rose from the bed. She moved with a fluid, ghostly grace, stripping away the layers of her disguise—the skirt, the petticoats, the stockings, the nightgown that had served as her shroud. She pushed the heavy chest, laden with linens and her own form, against the far wall until it stood flush with the timber. Then, she glided to the threshold, pressing her ear to the wood, listening for the echo of footsteps. Silence answered her; the sounds of the household had faded into the night.

Within that chest lay a deception so profound it defied detection by any eye unaccustomed to the mechanics of survival. A section of the floorboards above had been fractured, and when Gerard had requested repairs to restore the room's dignity, lacking proper materials, he had ingeniously cut away a precise aperture. This opening was sized exactly to accommodate Margaret's slender frame, allowing her to slide beneath the planks while the stolen wood sealed the gap behind her. The chest itself, appearing merely a foot deep, actually rested on the rafters two feet below the surface, creating a hollow tomb disguised as furniture.

Now, under the cover of absolute stillness, Margaret knelt and offered a silent prayer to the heavens. Rising, she crept to the edge of the hidden cavity and whispered, tenderly, "Gerard."

There was no response. She pressed her voice slightly higher, desperation creeping into her tone. "Gerard, all is safe. Thank Heaven! You may rise; but oh, be cautious!"

Silence hung heavy in the air. She placed her trembling hand upon his shoulder. "Gerard!"

Still nothing. Panic, cold and sharp, pierced her resolve. "Oh, what is this?" she cried, her fingers flying wildly across his face, searching his chest for a pulse. She gripped his shoulders, shaking him violently, lifting him as if he weighed nothing more than a bundle of rags. But he did not stir. He slid from her grasp, falling back not with the resistance of a living man, but with the final, weightless collapse of a corpse.

A primal dread seized her. The lid had been down. She had lain upon him. The intruders had occupied the room for some time. With the frenzied strength of a cornered animal, she tore him from the darkness of the chest and dragged him to the window. She flung the sash wide, inviting the cool, fragrant night air to rush in. She laid him there, exposed to the silver wash of the moonlight.

His complexion was the color of ash; his limbs were slack, utterly devoid of motion. She pressed her palm to his breast. Horror! It was as still as death itself. The horror of horrors washed over her: she had suffocated him with her own body. The human mind struggles to accept such a sudden, grotesque calamity. Gerard, who had barely managed to squeeze into that cramped confinement mere minutes prior, how could he already be dead?

She called out to him using every endearing name her heart could conjure, every phrase her tongue could frame. She kissed him, caressed him, coaxed him, imploring him to speak. There was no answer to words of love she had never dared utter before, nor ones she believed capable of escape. Trembling violently, she began to babble over his ashen features, words that were simultaneously terrible and pitiful.

"Oh, Gerard! I am so sorry you are dead. I am so sorry I have killed you. Forgive me for not letting the men take you; it would have been kinder than this. Oh, Gerard! I am very, very sorry for what I have done."

Suddenly, her composure shattered into madness. "No! No! Such things cannot be, or there is no God. It is monstrous! How can my Gerard be dead? How can I have killed my Gerard? I love him. Oh, God! You know how I love him. He does not. I never told him. If he knew my heart, he would speak to me; he would not be so deaf to his poor Margaret. Is it all a trick to make me cry out and betray him? But no! I love him too well for that. I'll choke myself first."

She seized her own throat, silencing the wild urge to scream in her terror and anguish. "If he would but say one word. Oh, Gerard! Don't die without a word. Have mercy on me and scold me, but speak to me! If you are angry with me, scold me! Curse me! I deserve it: the idiot who killed the man she loved better than herself. Ah, I am a murderess. The worst in all the world. Help! Help! I have murdered him. Ah! Ah! Ah! Ah! Ah!"

She tore at her hair, unleashing shrieks so wild, so piercing, they rang out like funeral knells, striking the ears of Dierich Brower and his men. Instantly, the group sprang to their feet, turning in unison, their faces illuminated by the shock of the sound.
